full_text: [TRANSLATION FAILED: Камрана Размовар приводит еще один страна аргумент...] [TRANSLATION FAILED: Но существование стран и народов так не устанавлив...] [TRANSLATION FAILED: А теперь давайте этот миф о Велико-Армении, состав...] [TRANSLATION FAILED: По утверждению Википедии, Велико-Армении существов...] [TRANSLATION FAILED: И где-то посередине вот этих вот 80 лет родился и ...] [TRANSLATION FAILED: Как ни странно ни один арминин не встретился Иисус...] [TRANSLATION FAILED: Нет никакой великой арминь есть десятки государств...] [TRANSLATION FAILED: Но нет ни армян, ни арминь, ни надо пихать это там...] [TRANSLATION FAILED: Ивангелий не является перечнем всех народов ближне...] Moreover, the name Arminya is recorded approximately 5 centuries before the birth of Jesus. Around 520 BC, Darius was the first to leave the Bihistus inscription. In the Drine Persian text the country is called “Armina of the South of Armenia”. The Iranica Encyclopedia translates the latter as Armenian. Now to the statement of the Comran that in the Bible there is armor, but there are no Armenians. Even this is not true when it comes to Bible translations in general. In the classic English translation of the King Yaklov Bible, book 4 of TsAS-19, chapter 37 of the element, and in the book “About Rock and Saee”, chapter 37 of the 38th element, the expression land of Armenia is directly used. In modern translations, the land “Arorad” is more often used in these same places. And this shows the main problem of the Comran argumate. Different linguistic and translation traditions can convey ancient geographical names in different ways. This can be seen even in the Bihistus inscription. Ancient Persisk versions use the name Armin o Vavilovskaya Uroshtu, that is, the old Mesaputan name "Urartu" existed early in the same region. There is independent Greek evidence. Herodotus from the fifth century BC mentions Armenians. At the beginning of the 4th century BC, Ksinovon repeatedly writes about Armenia and the Armenians. Therefore, the Komran question why Jesus did not meet the Armenians historically proves nothing. Persian and Glic sources document Armenia and the Armenians in the century before the birth of Christ. And the attempt to prove the absence of Armenia with the word “Ararat” collapses at the sources themselves. Comran simply mixes different linguistic traditions and takes the difference in name for the absence of a country.

Moreover, the name Arminya is recorded approximately 5 centuries before the birth of Jesus.
Around 520 BC, Darius was the first to leave the Bihistus inscription.
In the Drine Persian text the country is called “Armina of the South of Armenia”.
The Iranica Encyclopedia translates the latter as Armenian.
Now to the statement of the Comran that in the Bible there is armor, but there are no Armenians.
Even this is not true when it comes to Bible translations in general.

In the classic English translation of the King Yaklov Bible, book 4 of TsAS-19, chapter 37 of the element, and in the book “About Rock and Saee”, chapter 37 of the 38th element, the expression land of Armenia is directly used.
In modern translations, the land “Arorad” is more often used in these same places.
And this shows the main problem of the Comran argumate.
Different linguistic and translation traditions can convey ancient geographical names in different ways.
This can be seen even in the Bihistus inscription.
Ancient Persisk versions use the name Armin o Vavilovskaya Uroshtu,
that is, the old Mesaputan name "Urartu" existed early in the same region.
There is independent Greek evidence.
Herodotus from the fifth century BC mentions Armenians.
At the beginning of the 4th century BC, Ksinovon repeatedly writes about Armenia and the Armenians.
Therefore, the Komran question why Jesus did not meet the Armenians historically proves nothing.
Persian and Glic sources document Armenia and the Armenians in the century before the birth of Christ.
And the attempt to prove the absence of Armenia with the word “Ararat” collapses at the sources themselves.
Comran simply mixes different linguistic traditions and takes the difference in name for the absence of a country.
